name: small-object-optimization
intent: Keep a small payload inside the object that owns it - a fixed, in-object buffer - and fall back to a heap allocation only when the payload outgrows that buffer, so the typical small instance costs no allocator traffic and no pointer indirection.
problem: A type that owns variable-length data (a string, a byte buffer, a callable wrapper, a small vector, a record value) is usually constructed with payloads far below its worst case, yet the straightforward representation allocates on every construction: one heap block per instance, a pointer dereference per access, an owner to track, and an out-of-memory path for values that are tiny. The decision is whether to pay that allocation unconditionally, or to make the object bigger and smarter: reserve a fixed inline region that is part of the object, keep the small case there, and allocate only when a value actually exceeds the buffer. The trigger is a known or measured distribution of small payloads on a path where allocation cost, allocation failure, latency determinism or cache behaviour matters.
context: Applies where you define the type yourself - strings and byte buffers, type-erased wrappers (function/any-style containers), small vectors, record values, hot map keys - and the payload size distribution is dominated by small values. The payload must be movable (or byte-copyable) between the two representations, the extra bytes per object must be affordable, and the type must not cross a frozen ABI or serialization boundary where the buffer size would become a contract. It is a value-level layout decision local to one type's definition, not a structure spanning components.
benefits: The common small case performs no allocator call at all - no malloc/free traffic, no allocator metadata, no thread-local cache or lock hop - which is exactly where concurrent workloads suffer most.
Better locality: the payload lives in the same cache line as the object, so construction and the first access cost one memory touch instead of two dependent ones.
Deterministic cost: constructing, copying, moving and destroying a small instance cannot fail and cannot block on the allocator, which is what embedded, real-time and pre-allocated-pool systems need.

Cheap moves: the small case can be relocated by copying bytes (or by fixing one internal pointer), so moving a small value is allocation-free and can be noexcept; the large case stays a pointer hand-off.
Fewer allocations overall - the inline buffer absorbs the long tail of small values, cutting allocation count, fragmentation and per-allocation overhead.
Opt-in and invisible: the public contract is unchanged, so the optimization can be introduced, tuned or removed without touching callers.
tradeoffs: The inline buffer is part of every instance whether or not it is used: sizeof grows and every copy, move and destruction memcpys the whole object - pure loss for instances that spill and for instances that stay empty.

Two representations in one type: a discriminator decides inline versus heap, so every access branches, and both code paths must be written, kept consistent and tested (empty, exactly at capacity, grown, spilled, moved, copied).

The buffer size is a layout commitment: once it leaks into the ABI (as std::string's does across library builds) it cannot be tuned without breaking binary compatibility, and the same capacity decides how much of a cache line the object claims.

References and iterators into the payload behave differently in the two states: a spill or a move invalidates whatever pointed at the inline copy, and the payload's address can change although the object has value semantics.

Dense storage can regress: an array of objects that each carry a 24-byte buffer streams far more bytes than an array of small handles, so the optimization can lose against the representation it replaces.
It only pays when small payloads dominate and allocation shows up in the profile; applied speculatively it is added complexity with an unmeasurable benefit and a larger object to move.

participants.responsibility: The type that owns the payload; its sizeof, alignment and move behaviour are what the pattern reshapes.
The fixed, correctly aligned storage region inside the object; it holds the payload while it fits and is otherwise idle.
The spilled form of the same logical value: a pointer (plus capacity and allocator) to separately owned storage.
The state that tells the access path which representation is live - a tag, a spare bit in a length field, or an encoded capacity.
The member functions (or the vtable of a type-erased wrapper) that present a single interface over both representations and implement the transition.
The rules that decide when a value spills, how the inline payload is relocated, and what remains valid across copy, move and swap.

use_cases: Strings and byte buffers in parsers, protocol codecs and log/telemetry pipelines where most values are short but a few are large.
Type-erased callables and value containers (function/any-style wrappers) whose stored targets are typically small captures or plain function pointers.
Small vectors and keys in hot maps - collections whose element count is usually 0-8 but which must not be capped.
Embedded and real-time components that must not allocate after startup yet still need variable-length fields whose typical size is known.
Cache-sensitive structures (order books, game entity components, column values) where per-instance pointers and allocations dominate the cost of resting data.
Reusable per-thread or per-connection scratch objects that hold short messages inline and grow only for the rare large payload.

llvm::SmallVector<T,N> and llvm::SmallString across the LLVM compiler: the Programmer's Manual prescribes them exactly where vectors are 'usually small' - a basic block's predecessor/successor lists are usually under 8 elements - so the malloc/free call never costs more than the code fiddling with the elements, at the explicit condition that the vector lives on the stack.

Folly's type-erased wrappers (Poly-based Function, exception_wrapper) store small callables and exceptions in-situ in a fixed inline buffer, which the library's own docs justify as removing the proliferation of shared_ptrs and unique_ptrs in APIs that heap-stored type erasure forces.
avoid_when: Payloads are usually larger than any sensible buffer: the representation then costs size and a branch for nothing - keep the plain heap form or reserve capacity once.
Allocation is not on the critical path: an arena (std::pmr/monotonic), an object pool or one long-lived buffer with reserved capacity removes the allocator without a second representation.
The type crosses a stable ABI or serialization boundary: the inline capacity becomes part of the contract and can never be tuned - prefer pimpl or an opaque handle.
Objects are stored densely and iterated linearly: a larger sizeof can hurt more than the avoided allocations save, so measure array-of-structs workloads first.
The language or runtime already handles it: JVM/JS/Go heaps plus JIT and escape analysis optimise non-escaping values and small allocations, and hand-rolled layouts there fight the runtime.
The payload is not movable or is address-sensitive (self-referential): relocating it between inline and heap storage is then unsafe or impossible.
anti_patterns: Adding an inline buffer to every small type 'for performance' without a size distribution: objects bloat, copies get slower and no allocation is actually saved.
Leaking the inline capacity into the ABI or the serialized form (public constant, wire field, sizeof-dependent allocation) so that tuning the buffer later becomes a breaking change.
Reimplementing the whole container around the buffer instead of using the platform's type-erased container or small-vector library.
Ignoring invalidation: caching a pointer into the payload across a spill, a move or a growth, or assuming the payload's address is stable because the type has value semantics.
Hand-rolling the union without alignment, placement-new lifetime and discriminator invariants - undefined behaviour presented as an optimization.
Using small object optimization as a remedy for a heap-heavy design: when instances are numerous and uniformly large, pooling or a different data layout is the real lever.
design_principles: Encapsulation: the representation and the buffer size are implementation details; the public contract must not expose them.
Optimize the common case: the frequent small path must be the allocation-free one; the rare large path may pay.
Single transition point: exactly one operation changes representation, so both states stay consistent by construction.
Value semantics preserved: copy, move, swap and destruction behave the same in both states, and cheap moves follow from the inline case.
Measure first: keep the simple representation whenever the payload distribution or the profile does not justify the buffer.
best_practices: Derive the inline capacity from a histogram of real payload sizes in the hot path, not from a round number, and keep it a private constant.
Prefer to hide the discriminator in spare bits of an existing field (length or capacity) so the object does not grow a separate tag word.
Implement one spill()/materialize() path and make the small path noexcept: no allocation, no throw for small values.
Handle alignment and lifetime explicitly: aligned storage or a union, placement new, std::launder where required, and exactly one destruction of the active member.
Test the boundary cases and the invalidation rules: empty, exactly at capacity, one byte over, spilled, moved-from, swapped, copied - and document what a spill does to references.
Reach for the platform's existing realization first (std::string/std::any/small_vector, [InlineArray], SmallVec, value classes) before writing a new buffer.
Validate with the array/iteration workload, not only per-object microbenchmarks, because sizeof and copying dominate in dense collections.

cppreference, std::any - 'Implementations are encouraged to avoid dynamic allocations for small objects, but such an optimization may only be applied to types for which std::is_nothrow_move_constructible returns true': https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/any

libstdc++ source, bits/basic_string.h - the small-string buffer as enum { _S_local_capacity = 15 / sizeof(_CharT) } over a union of _M_local_buf and _M_allocated_capacity, selected by _M_is_local(): https://github.com/gcc-mirror/gcc/blob/master/libstdc++-v3/include/bits/basic_string.h

Boost.Container small_vector header - 'small_vector is a vector-like container optimized for the case when it contains few elements. It contains some preallocated elements in-place': https://github.com/boostorg/container/blob/develop/include/boost/container/small_vector.hpp

cppreference, std::inplace_vector (C++26) - 'dynamically-resizable array with contiguous inplace storage. The elements of type T are stored and properly aligned within the object itself': https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/inplace_vector
docs.rs, smallvec - 'a certain number of elements inline, and fall back to the heap for larger allocations ... improving cache locality and reducing allocator traffic': https://docs.rs/smallvec
docs.rs, arrayvec - 'array-backed vector and string types, which store their contents inline': https://docs.rs/arrayvec

Swift standard library source, SmallString.swift - _SmallString stores a (UInt64, UInt64) bit pattern with capacity 15 code units on 64-bit platforms; StringObject.swift carries the isSmall discriminator: https://github.com/swiftlang/swift/blob/main/stdlib/public/core/SmallString.swift

LLVM Programmer's Manual, llvm/ADT/SmallVector.h - inline storage 'is good for vectors that are usually small (e.g., the number of predecessors/successors of a block is usually less than 8)'; the manual also warns that the inlined elements make the object large 'so you don't want to allocate lots of them': https://llvm.org/docs/ProgrammersManual.html

Folly docs, Poly.md - type-erasing wrappers 'can often store small objects in-situ, with no dynamic allocation', avoiding the proliferation of shared_ptr/unique_ptr in APIs; folly/ExceptionWrapper.h realizes the same pattern with an in-situ Buffer plus a VTable dispatch: https://github.com/facebook/folly/blob/master/folly/docs/Poly.md

rust-lang/rust issue #20198, 'String::as_mut_vec prevents small string optimization' - the documented counter-case: Rust's String stays heap-only because its API exposes the underlying byte vector, so an inline buffer would break ownership-transfer guarantees: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/20198
